questions.title: Why didn't the FBI's failure to meet FOIA's response deadline require disclosure here?
questions.question_body: The opinion says Farahi sued after the FBI missed FOIA's statutory deadline, but the case still turned entirely on whether Exemption 7(A) applied. I thought FOIA imposed strict time limits on agencies. If the FBI blew the deadline, why wasn't that enough to force production of the records? Is the only consequence that the requester can sue immediately, rather than any waiver of exemptions?

questions.title: How can appellate review be de novo if FOIA courts also defer to FBI and national-security declarations?
questions.question_body: The D.C. Circuit says it reviews summary judgment de novo, but then it also says the FBI gets deference because it is a law-enforcement agency, and even more deference when national security is involved. I'm having trouble reconciling those ideas. If review is truly de novo, what exactly is the court independently deciding, and what parts of the agency's affidavit-based showing are effectively taken at face value?

questions.title: What does 'compiled for law enforcement purposes' mean when the FBI says the file involves national security and terrorism?
questions.question_body: The court says Exemption 7(A) first requires the records to be 'compiled for law enforcement purposes,' and it cites the Pratt/Campbell requirement of a rational nexus to law-enforcement duties and a connection to a possible violation of law or security risk. In this case, the FBI referred to investigations of national security and international terrorism, plus Farahi's associations. Is that enough because terrorism is inherently criminal, or did the court need something more concrete than broad national-security concerns? I'm confused about where the line is between intelligence gathering and law enforcement for Exemption 7 purposes.

questions.title: Can an ongoing investigation by itself count as an 'enforcement proceeding' under FOIA Exemption 7(A)?
questions.question_body: I usually think of an 'enforcement proceeding' as a prosecution, an administrative case, or maybe immigration removal proceedings. But this opinion says that ongoing criminal investigations themselves count as proceedings for Exemption 7(A), so long as they are pending or reasonably anticipated. Is that a D.C. Circuit-specific rule, and how concrete does the future case have to be? For example, does the government need to identify a likely charge or tribunal, or is it enough to say it is still gathering evidence for a possible future case?

questions.title: Why was the 2023 Bender declaration enough when it sounds so conclusory about the investigation remaining ongoing?
questions.question_body: Farahi argued that too much time had passed and that the updated Bender declaration was very terse, just saying the relevant investigations 'remain ongoing.' The court basically agreed that it looked sparse in isolation, but then treated it as an update to the earlier, more detailed Hardy declarations. Is that a normal way for courts to evaluate agency affidavits in FOIA cases? At what point does an 'update' become too conclusory to carry the government's burden, especially where years have passed since the original showing?

questions.title: When may a FOIA court rely on sealed ex parte declarations without giving the requester access to them?
questions.question_body: A lot of the court's reasoning seems to depend on sealed, ex parte declarations that Farahi could not see, especially on the nature of the investigation and segregability. I understand the practical problem that public explanation might reveal the very information the government wants to protect, but this still seems hard on the requester. What are the limits on using ex parte submissions in FOIA litigation? Does the requester's failure to object in the district court effectively waive any challenge, or do courts still have an independent duty to be skeptical before relying on secret affidavits?

questions.title: What is a valid 'category-by-category' withholding explanation in FOIA, and why did the court say Farahi forfeited this issue?
questions.question_body: The opinion briefly mentions that when an agency withholds documents by category instead of document-by-document, the categories must be 'sufficiently distinct' to let the court test the claimed exemptions. Farahi argued that the FBI had not adequately justified its categories, but the court said he forfeited that argument because he did not specifically explain why the categories were overbroad. What would a proper challenge have looked like here? Does a requester need to attack each category one by one, almost like arguing a Vaughn index entry?

questions.title: How can 10,000+ pages and 80 CDs contain no reasonably segregable nonexempt information?
questions.question_body: The segregability holding is what confuses me most. The FBI located about 10,750 pages and 80 CDs, and the court still accepted that no meaningful nonexempt information was reasonably segregable from the withheld material. I understand that isolated words or phrases don't have to be released if they are just random scraps, but it still seems intuitive that some factual material should be separable from exempt material in a file that large. How do courts decide when nonexempt information is too intertwined to require disclosure, and how much explanation must the agency give to justify withholding entire records?
